title: Permission to use images, music, code and names

sources.claim: Registering a business name with a state, a DBA, or a domain name is not the same as trademark rights; federal registration is a separate process, and rights can also arise from actual use of a mark in commerce.

Fair use (17 U.S.C. section 107) is judged case by case using four factors: purpose and character of the use, nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market for the original. Giving credit does not by itself make a use fair; other bases for use are permission or a license, or a public-domain work.

sections.skill: Get permission or a license for images, music, code and names

questions.prompt: Is "I found it on Google" permission to use a photo?

choices.text: Yes, anything online is free to use
Yes, if the photo is small

questions.intro: Things you find online are usually owned by someone. Using another person's PHOTO, MUSIC, ARTWORK, written text or software CODE in your business generally needs PERMISSION, a LICENSE (written terms of use), or a source that clearly allows your kind of use. Public-domain works are free to use, and fair use is a narrow legal exception decided case by case; credit alone is not permission. "I found it on Google" is not permission. Read license terms: some allow only personal use, or require credit. Using another business's NAME or LOGO in a way that confuses customers can infringe trademark rights. Registering a business name, DBA or domain is not the same as trademark rights.

questions.prompt: Seeing the ladder means what?
questions.intro: If a neighbor's ladder is leaning against their house, you would not just take it because you can see it. You would ask, and maybe agree on when to return it. Photos, music and code online are like that ladder: being able to see them does not mean you may use them. A license is the neighbor's "yes" with the rules attached.
